title: Don't trust that red heart: what happens when you tap Like
sources: relay.dev/docs/guided-tour/updating-data/graphql-mutations/ (Relay, (c) Meta Platforms): 'Optimistic updates': 'if a user clicks the "Like" button, we would like to instantly show ... liked'; 'If the mutation ends up not succeeding, we would like to roll back that optimistic update'
react.dev/reference/react/useOptimistic: 'lets you optimistically update the UI'; example setOptimisticLike(true) then await saveChanges(); failed actions roll the UI back
Nielsen, 'Response Times: The 3 Important Limits' (nngroup.com, 1993): 0.1 s feels instantaneous; 1 s keeps flow of thought; 10 s keeps attention
teyro.app: coding track (web development, mobile apps), short daily lessons, real code with instant feedback

lines.text: Don't trust that red heart. | It's *lying* to you.
Here's what really happens | in the *first second* after you tap.
First, at *zero* milliseconds, | the heart turns red | before your phone has even *asked* the server.
Second, a tiny message leaves your phone, | saying *like this post,* | and travels to the server | while you're already *scrolling.*
Third, if that message fails, | say you lose signal, | the app quietly *rolls it back,* | or tries again later.
And finally, why? | Research says a *tenth of a second* feels *instant,* | and a trip to the server can take longer. | So the app *guesses* you'll succeed.
The full rule has *three* numbers. | A tenth of a second feels instant, | *one* second keeps your flow, | and after *ten* seconds, | people stop paying *attention.*
It's called *optimistic UI,* | and Meta's own developer docs | use the *Like* button as the example.
Try it. | Turn on *airplane mode,* | tap Like, | and watch what *your* app does.
If you want to build apps that feel this fast, | the app I learn on is in my *bio.*
